By abolishing state marriage recognition, we open the way for a legal system that respects all forms of peaceful adult association equally. You and those you love should be free to structure your lives without needing a government category to make your commitments “real.”

The Moral Principle: Adults Own Their Lives

Underneath all the legal details lies a simple moral principle:

Adults own their own lives.

That means they own their bodies, their choices, their time, and their relationships. They have the right to enter or exit relationships voluntarily, to make promises, to share property, to raise children, and to form families according to their own values.

The state’s job is not to bless those choices. The state’s job is to protect the rights of each person within them.

If two—or three, or more—consenting adults decide to live together, support each other, and call their union a marriage, that is their moral and social decision. A government stamp of approval adds nothing of value to their commitment. Its absence should not take anything away.

We do not need the state to tell us when love is real. We do not need it to define our families.

Answering the Fear: “But We’ve Always Done It This Way”

Some will say, “Marriage has always involved the state.” That is simply not true. Marriage long predates modern governments. It began as a private, social, and often religious institution. Communities, not bureaucracies, honored and enforced it.

Others will say, “If we give up state marriage, everything will be confusing.” But the truth is the opposite: right now, we are confused, because we mix emotional, spiritual, and legal questions into one overloaded concept.

By disentangling personal commitment from state regulation, we gain clarity:

  • The emotional and moral dimensions of marriage belong to individuals and communities.
  • The legal dimensions—property, contracts, caregiving, parenting—can be handled openly and directly, without pretending that one government status answers every question.

This is not chaos. It is honesty.

A Call for Courage and Consistency

If we say we believe in freedom, then we must apply that belief where it matters most: in the choices that shape our daily lives and deepest connections.

If we say we stand against discrimination, then we must stop using the state’s power to privilege one form of relationship and marginalize others.

If we say we value privacy, then we must stop inviting the government into our bedrooms, our living rooms, and our most intimate promises.

Abolishing state recognition and regulation of marriage is not an attack on marriage. It is a defense of marriage as a personal, voluntary, and human institution.

It is an insistence that love does not need a license.

It is a declaration that adults are competent to govern their own relationships, make their own commitments, and design their own lives—without a government script.

What We Should Demand

So what should we ask for?

  • Remove “marital status” as a legal gatekeeper for rights and benefits.
  • Replace marriage-based privileges with individual rights, partner designations, and enforceable contracts.
  • Leave the word “marriage” to people, communities, and faith traditions—to be defined and celebrated as they choose.
  • Commit to equal legal respect and protection for all peaceful, consensual adult relationships, without forcing them into a single state-approved mold.

This is not a small reform. It is a shift in how we understand the relationship between the individual and the state.

It is a statement that in the most personal sphere of all—who we love, how we live, whom we call family—the final authority does not belong to a legislature, a courthouse, or a bureaucratic form.

It belongs to us.

Let us have the courage to say: the state has no rightful place in licensing love. Let us build a legal order that protects people without prescribing how they must form their families. Let us finally liberate marriage from government control, and return it to where it has always truly belonged:

To the hearts, minds, and free choices of human beings.

The State Has No Place in the Bedroom: The Case for the Total Abolition of State Marriage Recognition

On a Tuesday morning in 2022, a 58-year-old woman in Ohio was denied the right to visit her partner of 32 years in the ICU, as he lay dying of COVID-19. The couple had raised three children together, shared a mortgage, filed joint tax returns, and considered themselves married in every sense of the word—but because they had never obtained a state-issued marriage license, hospital administrators, citing Ohio’s strict next-of-kin laws, barred her from his room. He died alone, and she was left to mourn a man the state refused to recognize as her husband.

This tragedy is not an anomaly. It is the inevitable product of a system with no root in justice, equity, or even the stated purpose of protecting vulnerable people: the state’s legal recognition and regulation of marriage. For centuries, the state has used the institution of marriage as a cudgel to enforce racial hierarchy, patriarchal control, and heteronormative conformity, while denying basic legal protections to millions of people whose relationships do not fit the state’s narrow, ahistorical definition of “valid.” The complete abolition of state marriage recognition—removing all legal ties to marital status, and treating all intimate, interdependent relationships solely as private, voluntary contracts—is the only just, liberty-affirming, and equitable framework for a pluralistic society. Marriage, at its core, is a personal promise between people who care for one another; it is not a license granted by the government, and it should never be treated as such.

State Marriage Was Born of Oppression, Not Protection

The modern institution of state-recognized marriage originated not as a celebration of personal commitment, but as a legal mechanism for patriarchal property transfer. For most of Western history, marriage was a contract between a father and a groom, in which a woman was treated as a chattel asset, transferred from one male owner to another with a dowry. Under the common law doctrine of coverture, enshrined in U.S. law until the late 19th century, married women had no independent legal personhood: they could not own property, sign contracts, keep their own wages, or even file for divorce without their husband’s consent. Marital rape was legally impossible, as a wife was considered her husband’s property to use as he saw fit. State marriage was not a shield for vulnerable partners; it was a tool to disenfranchise them.

This oppressive core persisted for centuries, as the state used marriage to enforce other forms of subjugation. Anti-miscegenation laws, which banned interracial marriage in 30 U.S. states until the Supreme Court struck them down in Loving v. Virginia (1967), were explicitly designed to preserve white supremacy by preventing Black people from forming legally recognized unions with white people. Bans on same-sex marriage, the law of the land in 45 states until Obergefell v. Hodges (2015), were explicitly rooted in the religious belief that queer relationships were “immoral,” with the state acting as the enforcer of a narrow, majoritarian set of moral values. Even today, state marriage laws discriminate against disabled people: a person receiving Supplemental Security Income (SSI) or Medicaid can lose all their benefits if they marry, even if their spouse is also low-income and unable to support them, a rule that forces disabled people to choose between essential healthcare and forming a committed relationship. The state’s historical and ongoing involvement in marriage has never been about protecting people; it has always been about controlling who is allowed to access basic rights, and who is punished for stepping outside the state’s preferred social norms.

State Gatekeeping Guarantees Arbitrary Discrimination

Even when states expand their definitions of marriage to include previously excluded groups, the very act of state gatekeeping ensures that marginalized people are always left behind. The 2015 Obergefell decision, while a landmark victory for LGBTQ+ rights, was a half-measure that reinforced the state’s power to decide which relationships “count.” It did nothing to legalize polygamous marriage, leaving polyamorous people—who form long-term, committed, interdependent relationships with multiple partners, raise children together, and share finances and care responsibilities—denied every legal protection of marriage, even when their relationships are every bit as stable and loving as a monogamous dyad. It did nothing to extend marriage benefits to platonic life partners: two elderly sisters who have lived together for 50 years, shared a home, cared for each other through illness, and named each other as beneficiaries in their wills, are still denied the same tax benefits, Social Security survivor benefits, and hospital visitation rights that a newlywed couple of strangers would receive, simply because they are not romantically involved.

The patchwork of state marriage rules across the U.S. creates further arbitrary inequities. Some states recognize common-law marriage for long-term cohabiting partners; others do not, meaning a couple’s legal rights can depend entirely on which side of a state line they live on. Low-income people are also systematically harmed by the state’s marriage regime: the high cost of formal marriage—wedding licenses, ceremony costs, legal fees for prenuptial agreements—creates a de facto wealth barrier to accessing basic rights, privileging middle and upper-class couples. And even for couples who can afford to marry, the “marriage penalty” in the U.S. tax code means that nearly 20% of married couples pay more in taxes than they would as single filers, a punitive rule that disproportionately penalizes dual-income middle-class households. For immigrants, marriage is often the only viable pathway to citizenship, a system that traps thousands of people in abusive relationships every year: a spouse with a temporary visa may be afraid to leave an abuser, because doing so would mean deportation and separation from their children, with no pathway to legal status on their own. The state’s role as the sole arbiter of which relationships deserve legal recognition is not a neutral administrative function; it is a system of privilege that punishes anyone who does not fit the narrow mold of a monogamous, cisgender, heterosexual, middle-class couple.

State Marriage Ties Basic Rights to Arbitrary Status, Undermining Liberty and Safety

There is no legitimate reason to tie the legal protections currently associated with marriage to marital status at all. Every right that married people currently enjoy can be made available to any person in an interdependent, committed relationship through private, voluntary contract, without any state involvement in defining the relationship. Want hospital visitation rights for your partner? Sign a healthcare proxy naming them as your medical decision-maker, a document that is already legally valid in all 50 states. Want to inherit your partner’s property without a will? Sign a cohabitation agreement outlining property division and inheritance rights. Want to claim your partner’s Social Security benefits after they die? Name them as a beneficiary on your policy. None of these require a marriage license, and making them universally available, regardless of relationship status, would eliminate the arbitrary barriers that currently keep millions of people from accessing basic protections.

The current system of tying rights to marital status also actively harms vulnerable people, particularly survivors of domestic abuse. Because so many legal protections—housing rights, child custody, healthcare access, immigration status—are tied to marriage, abuse survivors are often trapped in violent relationships, unable to leave without losing everything. A 2022 study by the National Network to End Domestic Violence found that 1 in 3 domestic violence survivors stay with their abuser longer than they want to because they cannot afford to lose the health insurance, housing, or child custody rights tied to their marital status. Removing state marriage recognition would eliminate this coercive power: survivors would be able to leave abusive relationships without forfeiting their basic rights, because those rights would no longer be contingent on staying married.

Moreover, the current system wastes enormous state resources on a function that is entirely unnecessary. State governments spend millions of dollars every year administering marriage licenses, tracking marital status, enforcing marriage-based laws, and litigating disputes over who is “legally married.” This is a purely bureaucratic function that serves no public purpose: the state does not need to approve a person’s choice of romantic or platonic partner, any more than it needs to approve their choice of friends or business partners. Eliminating state marriage recognition would free up these resources to be used for actual public goods, like funding domestic violence services, expanding healthcare access, or reducing poverty.

Abolishing State Marriage Upholds Liberty, Pluralism, and the First Amendment

The state’s involvement in marriage is not just unjust in practice; it is a fundamental violation of the core principles of a free, pluralistic society. The First Amendment prohibits the state from establishing a religion, or favoring one set of religious beliefs over another—yet by defining what counts as a “valid” marriage, the state is inevitably taking a side in a deeply moral and religious debate. For some religious groups, marriage is exclusively a union between one man and one woman; for others, it is a union between two people of any gender; for others still, it is a union between multiple partners, or even a platonic spiritual bond. By enshrining one definition of marriage in law, the state is either privileging the beliefs of one group over all others, or forcing religious institutions to act against their beliefs. For example, during the fight over same-sex marriage, conservative bakers, florists, and churches argued that being forced to provide services for same-sex weddings violated their religious freedom, while LGBTQ+ couples argued that being denied the right to marry was a violation of their equal rights. This conflict existed entirely because the state was the gatekeeper of marriage. If the state has no role in recognizing marriage at all, both sides get what they want: religious groups can define and perform marriage according to their own beliefs, and LGBTQ+ people, polyamorous people, and all other groups can form the relationships they want, without the state interfering.

Abolishing state marriage recognition would also end the endless culture wars that have consumed American politics for decades. Debates over same-sex marriage, polygamy, trans people’s right to marry, and even the “definition of marriage” have become flashpoints for political division, with both sides fighting to control the state’s power to define a deeply personal institution. Removing the state from the equation eliminates the stakes of these fights: no one is fighting over who gets access to state-sponsored privileges, because there are no state-sponsored privileges tied to relationship status. This would free up political energy to focus on issues that actually affect all people, like economic inequality, healthcare, and climate change, rather than wasting time on culture war battles over who is allowed to be loved and recognized by the state.

Rebutting Common Counterarguments

Critics often argue that abolishing state marriage would leave vulnerable people, particularly children and low-income partners, without necessary legal protections. But this argument rests on a false premise: that the only way to protect vulnerable people is to tie those protections to state-recognized marriage. In reality, all the legal protections that currently benefit married couples can be made available to anyone who needs them, regardless of relationship status, through targeted, status-neutral laws. To protect children of non-marital parents, states can implement automatic legal guardianship for any adult who is the primary caregiver of a child for more than six months, regardless of marital status. To protect low-income interdependent partners, states can implement default inheritance and property division rules for cohabiting partners who have lived together for more than two years, without requiring a marriage license. None of these reforms require state marriage recognition, and all of them would be more equitable than the current system, which only provides protections to people who fit the state’s narrow definition of marriage.

Another common counterargument is that state marriage promotes social stability by incentivizing long-term commitment. But there is no empirical evidence that state recognition of marriage makes relationships more stable. The U.S. divorce rate hovers around 40% for first marriages, and studies have found that the availability of state marriage benefits has no significant impact on whether couples stay together. In fact, the state’s marriage regime often undermines stability by penalizing low-income couples who cannot afford to marry, or by forcing people to stay in abusive relationships to avoid losing benefits. Stability comes from voluntary commitment, mutual care, and access to resources like healthcare and economic security—not from a state-issued license.

Conclusion

For too long, the state has overstepped its bounds by inserting itself into the most personal, intimate part of human life: the relationships we build with the people we love. The institution of state marriage is a relic of a patriarchal, racist, heteronormative past, a system that has never been about protecting people, but about controlling them. It discriminates against marginalized groups, punishes disabled and low-income people, traps abuse survivors in violent relationships, and fuels endless culture wars over who is worthy of state recognition.

Abolishing state marriage recognition does not mean abolishing marriage as a personal commitment. It does not mean that people cannot have weddings, or make vows to each other, or build lives together. It simply means removing the state from the equation, so that no government official has the power to decide which relationships are “valid” and which are not. It means that all people, regardless of their race, gender, sexuality, relationship structure, or economic status, have equal access to the legal protections they need to care for themselves and their loved ones. It means that marriage, finally, can be what it was always meant to be: a private promise between people, free from state interference, free from discrimination, and free from the weight of centuries of oppression. It is time to take marriage out of the legal sphere entirely, and return it to the people, where it belongs.

Introduction

The licensing of marriage is a historical anomaly that emerged from now-discredited concerns about racial mixing and eugenics, not from any legitimate governmental interest.

The principle of equal treatment under law is actually violated, not upheld, by state involvement in marriage. Ending Culture Wars

Perhaps no issue has consumed more political energy in recent decades than battles over marriage definition. Privatizing marriage would instantly defuse these conflicts. Without state recognition to fight over, different communities could practice their own understanding of marriage without imposing it on others or feeling threatened by others' practices.

Religious conservatives could maintain traditional marriage within their communities without feeling that their values are under assault by state redefinition. The current one-size-fits-all marriage model poorly serves the diverse needs of modern relationships. State-defined marriage bundles together numerous legal provisions—inheritance rights, medical decision-making, property ownership, tax treatment—that couples may want to unbundle or customize. Consider a couple where one partner has children from a previous relationship. They might want to share some financial responsibilities but keep inheritance separate. The current binary system—married or not married—cannot accommodate such nuanced needs. Private contracts could.

The marriage industry costs taxpayers billions in administrative expenses, court costs for divorces, and tax revenue lost to marriage-based deductions and benefits. Family courts are clogged with divorce proceedings that could be handled through private arbitration. Government bureaucracies devoted to processing marriage licenses and maintaining records could be eliminated.

Moreover, the current system creates perverse economic incentives. Marriage penalties in the tax code discourage some couples from marrying, while benefits create incentives for fraud through marriages of convenience. Employer-provided spousal benefits create labor market distortions. All these inefficiencies would disappear if marriage were privatized.

Every legal protection currently provided by marriage could be better achieved through private contracts and targeted legislation. Hospital visitation? The privatization of marriage represents not a radical departure but a return to principles of individual liberty, religious freedom, and limited government. It would end destructive culture wars, provide superior legal flexibility, eliminate economic inefficiencies, and treat all citizens equally regardless of relationship status.

The answer, emphatically, is no. It's time to complete the separation of marriage and state, just as we've separated church and state. Let people commit to each other as they choose, worship as they choose, and contract as they choose—without requiring permission or recognition from government bureaucrats.

Marriage is too important to be left to the state. It's time to set marriage free.

Model Response:

The Case for Abolishing State-Recognized Marriage

Why Government Has No Business in Our Most Personal Relationships

For centuries, the state has inserted itself into one of humanity's most intimate institutions—marriage—claiming authority over who may form a family, under what conditions, and with what consequences. This arrangement, so deeply embedded in our legal and cultural architecture that most people never think to question it, is in fact an extraordinary overreach of governmental power. The time has come to argue what an increasing number of legal scholars, libertarians, progressives, and even some conservatives have begun to recognize: the state should exit the marriage business entirely. Marriage should be abolished as a legal category, replaced by private contracts and voluntary arrangements between consenting adults, while the legitimate legal functions currently bundled into marriage should be disaggregated and addressed through neutral, universally accessible legal instruments.

This is not an argument against marriage itself. People will continue to marry in churches, temples, mosques, backyards, and beaches. They will continue to make vows, wear rings, and celebrate unions. What they should stop doing is seeking permission from the government to do so, and what the government should stop doing is distributing a sprawling package of legal privileges and penalties based on a single, one-size-fits-all institution rooted in religious tradition and historical property arrangements.

I. The Historical Case: Marriage as a Tool of State Control

To understand why abolition is warranted, one must first understand how state marriage came to exist. Marriage was not always a legal institution. For most of human history, it was a private, familial, and religious matter. The state's involvement in marriage is a relatively modern phenomenon, accelerating in the West during the early modern period when governments began requiring licenses and registrations.

The motivations behind state involvement were rarely noble. Colonial and early American marriage laws were designed to enforce racial hierarchies, prevent miscegenation, regulate the transfer of property between men, and establish women as legal dependents of their husbands under the doctrine of coverture. Marriage law was, in its origins, a mechanism for controlling sexuality, reproduction, property, and racial purity. The English common law tradition that American law inherited treated a married woman as legally dead—her property, her earnings, her body, and even her children belonged to her husband.

While marriage law has been reformed dramatically since those early days—coverture has been abolished, marital rape has been criminalized, interracial marriage has been legalized, and same-sex marriage has been recognized—the fundamental structure remains: the state decides who may marry, grants a license, and then attaches to that license an enormous bundle of over one thousand federal legal consequences, from tax filing status to immigration rights to hospital visitation to inheritance to Social Security survivor benefits. The progressive reforms of marriage law have been real and important, but they have also obscured a deeper question: why should the state be in this business at all?

The history of state marriage is not a history of the government protecting love. It is a history of the government using an intimate institution as a vehicle for social engineering, demographic management, and the enforcement of majoritarian moral norms. Every expansion of marriage rights—to interracial couples, to same-sex couples—has been a battle fought against the state's previous use of marriage as a tool of exclusion. This pattern should make us deeply skeptical that the state can be trusted as a neutral custodian of this institution.

II. The Equality Argument: Marriage as a Source of Discrimination

One of the strongest arguments for abolishing state marriage is that it is inherently discriminatory. Marriage, as a legal institution, creates a two-tiered system of citizenship. Those who are married receive a vast array of benefits and protections. Those who are not married—whether by choice, by circumstance, or because they structure their intimate lives differently—are treated as second-class citizens.

Consider the scope of this discrimination. Married couples receive preferential tax treatment in many circumstances. They receive automatic inheritance rights, hospital visitation rights, the ability to make medical decisions for an incapacitated partner, immigration sponsorship privileges, Social Security survivor benefits, veterans' benefits, employer-provided health insurance for spouses, and favorable treatment in bankruptcy, tort, evidence, and property law. These are not trivial advantages. They are fundamental legal protections that affect people's economic security, their health, their freedom, and their ability to care for the people they love.

Why should these protections be available only to people who happen to be in a specific type of romantic relationship recognized by the state? A single person who has devoted decades to caring for an aging parent cannot sponsor that parent for immigration benefits. Two siblings who have lived together for thirty years and built a shared economic life cannot file joint tax returns. A person in a committed but unmarried partnership may be barred from their partner's hospital room during a medical emergency. An elderly widow who falls in love again but does not wish to remarry—perhaps because remarriage would eliminate her survivor benefits from a deceased spouse—must choose between love and economic security.

The marriage equality movement, culminating in Obergefell v. Hodges (2015), was a monumental victory for LGBTQ+ rights. But the logic of that movement, if followed to its conclusion, points beyond expanding marriage to abolishing its legal privileged status. Justice Kennedy's majority opinion in Obergefell celebrated marriage as essential to human dignity and fulfillment. But if dignity and fulfillment are the values at stake, then surely those values are not exclusive to people in conjugal pairs. The polyamorous triad, the asexual life partnership, the close friends who have chosen to build a life together, the single person who finds fulfillment in community rather than coupledom—all of these people have equal claims to dignity. As long as marriage exists as a legal category, the state is making a normative judgment that one particular form of intimate life—the romantic, typically sexual, dyadic partnership—is superior to all others and deserves special recognition and reward. This is a judgment the state has no legitimate basis to make.

Scholars like Tamara Metz, in her book Untying the Knot, and Elizabeth Brake, who coined the term "minimal marriage," have argued persuasively that the current system of legal marriage constitutes what Brake calls "amatonormativity"—the systemic privileging of romantic love relationships over all other forms of human connection. This is not merely unfair to individuals; it distorts social policy by channeling benefits through a romantic gatekeeping mechanism rather than distributing them based on actual need, actual dependency, or actual care relationships.

III. The Liberty Argument: Marriage as Government Overreach

From a perspective of individual liberty, state marriage is difficult to justify. The government does not require a license for people to become friends. It does not issue permits for religious worship. It does not register people's philosophical beliefs or artistic partnerships. Yet it claims the authority to define, regulate, and license one of the most personal decisions a human being can make: with whom to share a life.

The libertarian case against state marriage is straightforward: relationships between consenting adults are none of the government's business. The state's role should be limited to enforcing contracts, protecting individual rights, and adjudicating disputes. All of these functions can be accomplished without the institution of marriage. If two people wish to create mutual obligations—shared property, medical decision-making authority, inheritance arrangements—they can do so through private contracts, powers of attorney, wills, trusts, and other legal instruments that are already available and that do not require the state to pass judgment on the nature of their relationship.

But the liberty argument extends beyond libertarian philosophy. Progressives and feminists have long recognized that state marriage can be a tool of oppression. The welfare system in the United States has historically penalized marriage among low-income people through benefit clawbacks, creating perverse incentives. At the same time, politicians regularly promote marriage as a solution to poverty—a deeply patronizing approach that places the burden of structural economic inequality on the intimate choices of individuals. The "marriage promotion" programs funded by the federal government since the 1990s have spent hundreds of millions of taxpayer dollars encouraging low-income people to marry, with negligible results, while ignoring the systemic causes of poverty. When the state is in the marriage business, marriage inevitably becomes a tool of social policy, and intimate relationships become instruments of governance.

Religious liberty is also implicated. When the state defines marriage, it inevitably comes into conflict with religious communities whose understanding of marriage differs from the state's definition. The post-Obergefell conflicts between same-sex marriage rights and religious objections—involving bakers, florists, county clerks, and adoption agencies—are a direct consequence of the state's involvement in marriage. If marriage were purely a private and religious matter, these conflicts would largely disappear. A church could define marriage according to its own theology without any implication that the state endorses or rejects that definition. A same-sex couple could marry in a welcoming congregation without needing the validation of a government that has historically excluded them. The culture war over marriage is, at its root, a war over state power—over who gets to control the legal definition of a word and an institution. Remove the state from the equation, and the war loses its battlefield.

IV. The Practical Case: Disaggregating the Marriage Bundle

Critics of marriage abolition often argue that marriage performs essential legal functions that cannot easily be replaced. This objection is serious but ultimately unpersuasive. The legal functions currently bundled into marriage can be disaggregated and provided through other means—means that would be more flexible, more inclusive, and more precisely tailored to the actual needs they serve.

Property and Economic Partnership. Married couples currently receive default rules governing shared property, debt, and economic dissolution (divorce). These functions can be served by domestic partnership contracts or civil solidarity agreements—standardized, opt-in legal frameworks that any two or more people can enter into to govern their shared economic lives. These agreements would not require a romantic or sexual relationship. They could be used by romantic partners, by elderly siblings sharing a home, by friends co-parenting a child, or by any other configuration of people who wish to formalize their economic interdependence. France's PACS (Pacte civil de solidarité), originally introduced as an alternative to marriage for same-sex couples, has become enormously popular among heterosexual couples as well, demonstrating that people will enthusiastically adopt flexible legal frameworks when offered the choice.

Medical Decision-Making and Hospital Visitation. These rights can be assigned through durable powers of attorney for healthcare, advance directives, and designated healthcare proxies. These instruments already exist and are already used by unmarried people. Making them more accessible, more affordable, and more widely understood would be far more equitable than tying these fundamental rights to marital status.

Inheritance. Wills, trusts, and beneficiary designations already allow individuals to direct the distribution of their property after death. Default intestacy rules could be reformed to recognize designated legal partners or dependents rather than relying on marital status as a proxy.

Taxation. The joint filing system for married couples is widely criticized by tax scholars as inefficient, regressive, and distortionary. It creates the so-called "marriage penalty" for some couples and a "marriage bonus" for others, based not on any coherent policy rationale but on the accident of how two incomes interact with a progressive rate structure. Abolishing joint filing and taxing all individuals as individuals would be simpler, fairer, and more efficient. To the extent that the tax code should account for dependency relationships, it can do so directly—through dependent deductions and credits—without reference to marriage.

Immigration. Spousal immigration sponsorship is one of the most commonly cited reasons for preserving legal marriage. But the current system is already deeply flawed. It creates enormous incentives for marriage fraud, leads to years-long bureaucratic investigations into the "legitimacy" of marriages, and traps some immigrant spouses in abusive relationships because their immigration status depends on their marriage. A reformed immigration system could allow sponsorship based on demonstrated genuine relationships of dependency and commitment, evaluated through objective criteria, rather than relying on the crude proxy of a marriage certificate.

Children. Parentage law is already substantially independent of marriage law. Unmarried parents have legally recognized rights and obligations. Child support, custody, and visitation are determined based on the best interests of the child, not the marital status of the parents. Fully decoupling parentage from marriage would complete a process that is already well underway and would ensure that all children receive equal legal protection regardless of whether their parents are married.

Social Security and Benefits. Survivor benefits for spouses and dependents can be reformed to cover designated dependents or legal partners, rather than limiting them to married spouses. This would extend protection to many people who currently fall through the cracks—unmarried long-term partners, dependent adult children with disabilities, and others who are genuinely dependent but lack the marriage credential.

The point is not that these reforms would be trivially easy to implement. Legal transitions of this magnitude are always complex. The point is that every function currently served by marriage can be served better—more equitably, more flexibly, more precisely—by targeted legal instruments that do not require the state to define and regulate intimate relationships.

V. The Philosophical Case: The State Should Not Define Intimate Life

At the deepest level, the case for abolishing state marriage rests on a philosophical principle: the state should not be in the business of defining the good life. A liberal democratic government derives its legitimacy from its commitment to protecting individual rights and remaining neutral among competing conceptions of human flourishing. When the state establishes marriage as a privileged legal institution, it violates this neutrality. It declares that one form of intimate life—the conjugal pair—is officially endorsed, rewarded, and promoted, while all other forms are officially disfavored.

This is not a merely theoretical concern. The social and psychological effects of this endorsement are real. Single people report feeling stigmatized and marginalized by a culture that treats marriage as the default marker of adult success. Unmarried couples face social pressure to marry, not because marriage would serve their needs, but because it carries social and legal legitimacy that their relationship otherwise lacks. People in non-traditional relationship structures—polyamorous relationships, queer chosen families, platonic life partnerships—are rendered invisible by a legal system that recognizes only one model.

The philosopher Elizabeth Brake argues that the state's promotion of marriage constitutes a form of discrimination analogous to the establishment of religion. Just as the state should not declare one religion to be the official faith, it should not declare one form of intimate association to be the official relationship. The comparison is apt. Marriage, for many people, is a profoundly religious institution. For others, it is a secular commitment. For still others, it is irrelevant to their understanding of a good life. A just state respects all of these perspectives equally.

VI. Responding to Objections

"Marriage provides stability for children." The evidence on this point is more complicated than marriage proponents suggest. Research shows that what benefits children is not marriage per se but stable, loving, well-resourced households. Children in stable unmarried households do as well as children in married households when income and education are controlled for. The correlation between marriage and child wellbeing is largely a reflection of the economic advantages that the state confers on married couples—advantages that, under the abolitionist proposal, would be available to all caregiving households regardless of the adults' relationship status.

"Marriage is a fundamental human institution that predates the state." Precisely. If marriage predates the state, then it does not need the state. Religious and cultural communities successfully sustained marriage for millennia without government licenses. They can continue to do so. Abolishing state marriage does not abolish marriage; it returns marriage to the communities and individuals to whom it belongs.

"This is politically unrealistic." Perhaps in the short term. But the trajectory of social change suggests otherwise. The percentage of American adults who are married has declined from over 70% in 1960 to under 50% today. The percentage of children born to unmarried parents has risen dramatically. Cohabitation without marriage has become a mainstream lifestyle choice. Public attitudes toward marriage are evolving rapidly. The legal and cultural infrastructure of compulsory marriage is already crumbling. The question is not whether the state's role in marriage will diminish, but whether we will manage this transition thoughtfully and equitably or allow it to happen haphazardly, leaving vulnerable people without legal protection.

"The administrative burden of replacing marriage with individual contracts would be enormous." This concern is legitimate but overstated. Default legal frameworks—standardized partnership agreements that people can opt into with minimal paperwork—could replicate most of the convenience of marriage while offering far greater flexibility. The administrative complexity of the current system—with its marriage licenses, divorce courts, prenuptial agreements, and endless litigation over marital property—is already enormous. A system of clear, modular legal instruments might well be simpler to administer than the baroque edifice of current marriage law.

VII. Conclusion: Toward a More Just and Free Society

The abolition of state-recognized marriage is not a radical proposal. It is the logical conclusion of principles that most Americans already hold: that the government should respect individual liberty, that all citizens deserve equal treatment under the law, that intimate relationships are private matters, and that legal protections should be available to everyone who needs them, not only to those who conform to a particular model of domestic life.

Marriage is beautiful. Marriage is meaningful. For millions of people, it is a source of profound joy, commitment, and spiritual fulfillment. None of that requires a government license. None of that is diminished by removing the state from the equation. If anything, marriage is ennobled when it is chosen freely, for its own sake, without the distorting influence of legal privileges and penalties.

Let churches marry. Let synagogues marry. Let mosques marry. Let individuals design their own ceremonies, make their own vows, and define their own commitments. And let the state do what it does best—or at least what it should do best: protect individual rights, enforce voluntary agreements, and treat all citizens as equals before the law.

The state has no business in the bedrooms, the hearts, or the love stories of its citizens. It is time, at last, to untie the knot.

A speech advocating for the abolition of state-recognized marriage

Friends, fellow citizens, lovers of liberty—

Healthcare access, tax status, immigration rights, hospital visitation, inheritance, parental presumption—all gated behind a single institution that the state controls.

I am arguing against state marriage—the legal institution, the licensing regime, the governmental apparatus that has wrapped itself around something that belongs to individuals, families, communities, and churches.

The couple whose deeply-held commitment ceremony isn't recognized because it doesn't fit the state's template. The widow who loses benefits because the government never approved of her partnership. The person trapped in an abusive marriage who must navigate a costly, adversarial legal process just to regain their own autonomy.

Religious communities get hurt too. When the state defines marriage, it inevitably collides with religious definitions. Remove the state from the equation, and every church, mosque, temple, and synagogue is free to define and sanctify marriage according to its own beliefs—without government interference and without imposing on anyone else.

These tools already exist. We simply need to make them accessible, affordable, and robust—available to any two or more people who wish to formalize obligations to one another, regardless of whether their relationship is romantic.

Why should your elderly mother have fewer legal tools to designate you as her decision-maker than your spouse has? Why should two lifelong friends who own a home together have fewer protections than a married couple? We gain a government that is neutral on how you structure your personal life. Not hostile. Not prescriptive. Neutral.

We gain religious liberty in its fullest expression—communities free to celebrate marriage on their own terms without fearing that the state will redefine their sacraments or that their definitions will be imposed on others.

We gain genuine equality—not the kind where we fight every decade for a new group to be admitted to a government institution, but the kind where the government simply has no business being the gatekeeper of your intimate life in the first place.

We gain individual sovereignty over the most personal decision a human being can make.

We accept that a judge must approve your decision to leave. We accept that the state distributes fundamental rights—the right to visit your dying partner, the right to make medical decisions for your family—based on whether you've completed the proper paperwork with the county clerk.

That is radical. We've just been living with it so long we stopped noticing.

It is time to overcome the assumption that the government belongs in your marriage.

Love is not a license. Commitment is not a contract with the state. Family is not a category defined by bureaucrats.

These things belong to you.

Let us build a system that finally reflects that truth. Let us get the state out of marriage—not because marriage doesn't matter, but because it matters too much to leave in the hands of government.

Thank you.
